paper.abstract:
Abstract Flow matching has emerged as a powerful generative family for simulation-based inference (SBI).
However, sampling and density evaluation require numerical integration at inference time.
This makes posterior sampling in neural posterior estimation costly. More importantly, it can make repeated likelihood evaluation prohibitively expensive and impractical for Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, which may require thousands of repeated density evaluations.
Here, we develop conditional mean flows for posterior and likelihood approximation, combining few-step sampling with tractable density evaluation.
We show that the mean flow objective identifies conditional flow maps and that independent masking enables direct estimation of marginal likelihoods. We evaluate both posterior and likelihood estimation across several tasks and show that conditional mean flows retain the flexibility of flow-based density estimators while significantly reducing inference time. In particular, single-step conditional mean flow density evaluation yields estimation error comparable to 200-step flow matching while enabling about 200-fold faster downstream MCMC sampling.

sections.heading: 1 INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Mechanistic simulators are used to describe processes ranging from cognitive science ( Ratcliff et al., 2016 ) to disease modeling ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . Yet, while practically important, their likelihoods are often unavailable in closed form. Simulation-based inference ( Sisson et al., 2018 ; Cranmer et al., 2020 ; Deistler et al., 2025 ; Arruda et al., 2026 , SBI;) addresses this challenge by using simulated parameter-observation pairs ( 𝜽 , 𝐲 ) (\bm{\theta},\mathbf{y}) to infer unknown parameters, and amortized methods reuse the trained network across datasets ( Bürkner et al., 2023 ) . Two popular forms of SBI are neural posterior estimation (NPE) and neural likelihood estimation (NLE). NPE learns a posterior model q 𝝍 ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 ) q_{\bm{\psi}}(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}) which can sample from the approximate posterior directly. NLE, instead, learns a likelihood model q 𝝍 ​ ( 𝐲 ∣ 𝜽 ) q_{\bm{\psi}}(\mathbf{y}\mid\bm{\theta}) which requires Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample from the posterior. NPE amortizes over datasets but is usually tied to the prior and data format used in training, whereas NLE needs MCMC for every dataset, but allows the prior to be changed after training and composes exchangeable likelihoods across any number of i.i.d. observations ( Cranmer et al., 2020 ) . Many SBI methods demand neural estimators that are both flexible and inexpensive to evaluate. In NLE, MCMC requires thousands of likelihood evaluations per posterior, making each evaluation a practical bottleneck. Further, hierarchical approaches ( Arruda et al., 2024 ) or self-consistency objectives that improve NPE ( Schmitt et al., 2024a ; Mishra et al., 2026 ) and enable model comparison ( Kucharský and Bürkner, 2026 ) rely on density evaluation during training or inference. So far, normalizing flows have been a standard choice in these applications because they evaluate densities in a single pass ( Papamakarios et al., 2021 ; Dinh et al., 2017 ; Durkan et al., 2019 ) . However, their transformations must remain invertible with tractable Jacobians, which restricts how inductive biases can be built into the architecture ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Autoregressive flows based on causal transformers (e.g., TARFlow and STARFlow) relax this restriction ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) , but impose a fixed variable ordering and require sequential inversion for sampling. Moreover, tractable joint densities do not generally imply tractable marginals, which are required with missing observations ( Yalavarthi et al., 2024 ) . Flow matching and diffusion models instead learn a velocity or score field with an unconstrained neural network ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Wildberger et al., 2023 ; Sharrock et al., 2024 ; Arruda et al., 2026 ) , and diffusion transformers can flexibly represent arbitrary conditionals and marginals ( Gloeckler et al., 2024 ) . Yet, their densities require solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE), which can take hundreds of network evaluations and makes repeated likelihood calls during training or within MCMC costly. Few-step generative models reduce the sampling cost, but consistency models, for instance, provide no tractable density ( Song et al., 2023 ; Schmitt et al., 2024b ) . Thus, current SBI approaches either restrict the network architecture or make every density evaluation expensive . To overcome this limitation, we present conditional mean flows for SBI, which learn the average velocity between two times, so that one network evaluation defines a finite-time map based on mean flows ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ) . We first evaluate direct posterior sampling and density estimation, then focus on learned likelihoods for compositional inference, missing observations, and gradient-based and delayed acceptance MCMC. Concretely, we develop and showcase 1. a conditional mean flow formulation for posterior and likelihood approximation, with exact stepwise Jacobian determinants, and a proof that the mean flow objective suffices to identify conditional flow maps ( Section 3.1 , Proposition 1 ); 2. marginal density estimation for missing targets with a masked transformer backbone, and a proof that the masked objective targets the correct marginal likelihood ( Section 3.3 , Proposition 2 ); 3. and a benchmark against normalizing flows and regular flow matching on four tasks covering both NLE and NPE, including a single-trial likelihood comparison in which one mean flow step matches the error of 200-step flow matching with two orders of magnitude faster sampling ( Section 4 ); Figure 1: Learned two-moons posteriors as samplers and as densities. Top row: 5,000 draws per method for the canonical observation 𝐲 = ( 0 , 0 ) \mathbf{y}=(0,0) ; bottom row: the learned log-density on a 512 × 512 512{\times}512 grid with the exact 95% highest-density region dashed. ( A ) A normalizing flow; ( B ) a consistency model with S = 32 S{=}32 steps, which has no tractable density; ( C ) a mean flow with S = 1 S{=}1 . ( D ) The same mean flow with S = 32 S{=}32 and ( E ) a separately trained flow matching model integrated with 32 Euler steps. ( F ) The velocity head of the mean flow and ( G ) the flow matching model, both integrated with the adaptive Tsit5 ODE solver.

sections.heading: Simulation-based inference.
sections.text: For conditionally independent observations 𝐲 n \mathbf{y}_{n} , simulation-based inference targets p ⁡ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 obs ) ∝ p ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) ​ ∏ n = 1 N p ⁡ ( 𝐲 n ∣ 𝜽 ) p(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{obs}})\propto p(\bm{\theta})\,\prod_{n=1}^{N}p(\mathbf{y}_{n}\mid\bm{\theta}) when the likelihood is unavailable. Classical approximate Bayesian computation compares simulated and observed data directly, but becomes less effective as dimension increases ( Sisson et al., 2018 ) . Neural posterior estimation (NPE) fits q 𝝍 ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 ) q_{\bm{\psi}}(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}) to simulated pairs and draws approximate posterior samples without running MCMC for each dataset. Neural likelihood estimation (NLE), instead, fits a conditional density to prior-predictive pairs and uses it within MCMC ( Cranmer et al., 2020 , for an overview, see) . A per-observation estimator can be reused across dataset sizes, making single-trial likelihoods useful for models with exchangeable trials ( Boelts et al., 2022 ) , and spline coupling flows are the standard tractable-density baseline ( Durkan et al., 2019 ) .

sections.heading: Flow matching and diffusion-based inference.
sections.text: Flow matching learns a velocity field 𝐯 ⁡ ( 𝐳 t , t ) \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) that transports a Gaussian distribution to the target along a prescribed interpolation ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) . It has been applied to both NPE and NLE, alongside score-based generative models ( Arruda et al., 2026 , for a review, see) . Sampling requires ODE integration, and density evaluation additionally integrates the velocity divergence through the continuous change-of-variables formula ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , so repeated integration can dominate the cost of NLE.

sections.heading: Few-step generative models.
sections.text: Consistency models learn transitions from intermediate noisy states toward data, enabling generation in one or a few steps ( Song et al., 2023 ) . They also support fast posterior sampling in SBI ( Schmitt et al., 2024b ; Arruda et al., 2026 ) , although the standard formulation does not provide a tractable posterior density. Flow maps learn finite-time ODE transitions between arbitrary time pairs, and mean flows parameterize these maps through average velocities and can be trained without distillation ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ) . Rehman et al. (2026) combined mean flows with a cycle loss that encourages invertibility to obtain few-step densities for Boltzmann generators.

sections.heading: MCMC with learned and multi-fidelity likelihoods.
sections.text: The no-U-turn sampler ( Hoffman and Gelman, 2014 ; Betancourt, 2017 , NUTS;) uses density and gradient evaluations to construct proposals, and probabilistic programming frameworks allow learned likelihoods to enter these calculations as model components ( Carpenter et al., 2017 ) . Delayed acceptance MCMC uses a cheap approximation to screen proposals while leaving the fine target invariant ( Christen and Fox, 2005 ) . Moreover, its multilevel variant organizes several approximations ( Lykkegaard et al., 2023 ) , and related approaches in SBI use simulators at different resolutions ( Prescott and Baker, 2021 ; Tatsuoka et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: A note on notation.
sections.text: We write 𝐳 \mathbf{z} for the density target and 𝐱 \mathbf{x} for the conditioning variables. In posterior estimation , the network learns q 𝝍 ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 ) q_{\bm{\psi}}(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}) with parameters 𝐳 ≡ 𝜽 \mathbf{z}\equiv\bm{\theta} as the target and data 𝐱 ≡ 𝐲 \mathbf{x}\equiv\mathbf{y} as the condition. In likelihood estimation , it learns q 𝝍 ​ ( 𝐲 ∣ 𝜽 ) q_{\bm{\psi}}(\mathbf{y}\mid\bm{\theta}) with 𝐳 ≡ 𝐲 \mathbf{z}\equiv\mathbf{y} and 𝐱 ≡ 𝜽 \mathbf{x}\equiv\bm{\theta} . The same formulation applies to either direction by choosing the target and condition accordingly.

sections.heading: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.text: We evaluate direct posterior approximation on two moons and likelihood approximation on the three further benchmarks, where the learned densities enter MCMC. The benchmarks show the following: • Two moons : few steps give accurate samples, so sampling has only a minor speed-accuracy trade-off, and densities improve with more steps ( Section 4.1 ). • Cognitive model : exchangeable likelihoods yield precision comparable to 200-step flow matching with about 200 × 200\times faster MCMC ( Section 4.2 ). • Epidemic renewal : a masked transformer marginalizes missing observations and is more accurate than a normalizing flow ( Section 4.3 ). • g-and-k : at a shared budget, more draws beat more steps, and delayed acceptance MCMC is as accurate as NUTS without gradients ( Section 4.4 ). We compare samples with exact references using the classifier two-sample test ( Lopez-Paz and Oquab, 2017 , C2ST;) , and densities through the Hellinger distance ( Appendix B ). Reference-free evaluations use normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE), effective sample size (ESS) and predictive checks, and the calibration for every trained estimator is assessed using tests of accuracy with random points ( Lemos et al., 2023 , TARP;) prior to any other evaluation ( Table S1 ). Tasks, architectures and generative models are described in Appendix B to E . Figure 2: Composing one learned trial likelihood over N N trials of a cognitive model. ( C ) Posterior contraction relative to the prior. Lines show the mean over 10 independent datasets, bands the sample standard deviation.

sections.heading: Setup and baseline.
sections.text: The two moons task has a two-dimensional parameter and observation, a bimodal crescent posterior, and an exact likelihood and posterior sampler ( Greenberg et al., 2019 ; Lueckmann et al., 2021 ) . All methods learn the posterior direction and are sampled directly with 5,000 draws per dataset, which we score against 32,000 exact reference draws. We compare a conditional mean flow at step counts S ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } S\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} with three baselines: a conditional normalizing flow, a conditional consistency model as the established few-step method ( Song et al., 2023 ; Schmitt et al., 2024b ) , and a separately trained conditional flow matching model integrated with S S Euler steps or an adaptive Tsit5 solver ( Tsitouras, 2011 ) . We integrate the velocity head of the mean flow with the same Euler or adaptive scheme, which repurposes the mean flow as a flow matching model. For both the consistency model and the mean flow, we tuned the sampling schedule for each step count on held-out observations, which are disjoint from the evaluation datasets.

sections.heading: Sample quality.
sections.text: The conditional mean flow reaches a similar C2ST at every step count ( Figure 1 and Figure S1 A), so a single step suffices for sampling and already outperforms the normalizing flow ( 0.523 0.523 against 0.543 0.543 ). In contrast, the consistency model needs at least 4 steps to approach this accuracy, and both flow matching variants need at least 32 Euler steps. The adaptive solver further improves the accuracy, but requires more than 300 solver steps. Hence, the mean flow with S = 1 S{=}1 draws 5,000 samples about 23 times faster than flow matching with 32 Euler steps and 140 times faster than with the adaptive solver ( Figure S2 ). It is also about 6 times faster than the normalizing flow and only reaches its sampling time at S = 8 S{=}8 . Since the velocity head of the mean flow and the separately trained model perform similarly under both solvers, mean flow training does not seem to degrade the learned velocity field. The consistency model is also sensitive to its discretization exponent, whose candidates span a C2ST from 0.54 0.54 to 0.98 0.98 at S = 4 S{=}4 , whereas the EDM schedule of the mean flow changes the C2ST by at most 0.015 0.015 ( Table S3 ).

sections.heading: Density quality.
sections.text: In contrast to sampling, we find that additional mean flow steps improve the density, and the Hellinger distance to the exact posterior decreases with S S ( Figure S1 B and Table S4 ). With S = 1 S{=}1 , the mean flow places mass between the two modes ( Figure 1 C), but it still outperforms the normalizing flow. Euler integration of either velocity field remains less accurate than the mean flow with S ≥ 2 S{\geq}2 up to 32 steps. The adaptive solver is most accurate, with the velocity head of the mean flow ahead of the separately trained flow matching model. Moreover, the mean flow density is close to normalized, whereas the Euler densities overshoot unit mass by many orders of magnitude at S = 1 S{=}1 and remain far from normalized at S = 32 S{=}32 ( Table S4 ). We attribute this to the Euler scheme approximating both the trajectory and the divergence integral in ( 1 ), whereas the mean flow computes the exact Jacobian determinant of each step. The normalizing flow is exactly normalized, but its density shows fold artifacts and places mass outside the prior support ( Figure 1 A). Flow matching models with adaptive solvers provide the most accurate densities, but more than 300 steps per evaluation make them too expensive for repeated density evaluation.

sections.heading: Setup and baseline.
sections.text: The cognitive model describes two-alternative decisions as a Wiener first-passage process with drift ν \nu , boundary separation a a and non-decision time t 0 t_{0} ( Ratcliff et al., 2016 ) , and is a standard benchmark for learned single-trial likelihoods ( Fengler et al., 2021 ) . We train one conditional mean flow on the signed response time y = ( 2 ​ c − 1 ) ​ t y=(2c-1)\,t , with choice c ∈ { 0 , 1 } c\in\{0,1\} and response time t t , and compose the learned trial likelihood into joint posteriors over N ∈ { 4 , 16 , 64 , 256 } N\in\{4,16,64,256\} trials, which we sample with NUTS. Since a response cannot be faster than t 0 t_{0} , we truncate the prior of t 0 t_{0} at the fastest observed response time of each run. We compare mean flow step counts S ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } S\in\{1,2,4,8\} with a flow matching model integrated with 200 Euler steps.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: With S = 1 S{=}1 , the NRMSE and posterior contraction of the mean flow are comparable to the flow matching baseline at every N N ( Figure 2 , Table S5 and Figure S3 ), while sampling is 182 to 216 × 216\times faster ( Figure S2 D). Additional steps increase the cost and the number of convergence failures without clearly reducing the parameter error ( Figure S4 ). From all MCMC runs, 8.5 % 8.5\% failed to converge, and all failed runs used S ≥ 4 S\geq 4 ( Table S5 ). We attribute this to the fact that the mean flow is trained for few-step sampling and evaluation only, and hence the intermediate maps might be poorly trained and additional steps, unlike in the discretization of an ODE, need not reduce the approximation error. However, for every method the coverage of the 95% central interval decreases and the worst posterior predictive discrepancy increases with N N ( Figure 2 B). Composing many approximate likelihoods accumulates their errors while the posterior contracts, which makes even the 200-step baseline overconfident. With S = 1 S{=}1 , the additional discretization error further lowers the coverage at N = 256 N{=}256 , whereas with S = 2 S{=}2 coverage and predictive discrepancy are comparable to the baseline.

sections.heading: Setup and baseline.
sections.text: Since conditional mean flows do not constrain the network architecture, we can tailor the backbone to observations with missing entries. We consider a stochastic renewal process, a standard forward model for estimating time-varying reproduction numbers R t R_{t} ( Fraser, 2007 ; Cori et al., 2013 ; Gostic et al., 2020 ) , in which the incidence is driven by a generation-interval force (Appendix E.3 and Figure S5 ). The parameter is the 128-dimensional coefficient vector 𝐳 \mathbf{z} with log ⁡ R = L ​ 𝐳 \log R=L\mathbf{z} , where L L is the Cholesky factor of a squared-exponential kernel ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2005 ) , such that the prior is 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\mathbf{I}) . We withhold 30% of the observed steps completely at random and redraw this pattern for each dataset. Under this mechanism, inference only requires the marginal likelihood p ⁡ ( 𝐲 𝒪 ∣ 𝐳 ) p(\mathbf{y}_{\mathcal{O}}\mid\mathbf{z}) of the observed entries 𝒪 \mathcal{O} ( Little and Rubin, 2019 ) . We parameterize the mean flow with a masked transformer trained with missing coordinates and a causal mask over time. In contrast, the normalizing flow has a fixed input width, so we train and evaluate it with a value of − 1 -1 in the missing entries ( Figure S5 C). Both models are trained on a low budget of 8,192 simulations, and the mean flow is evaluated with S = 1 S{=}1 .

sections.heading: Posterior accuracy and sampling cost.
sections.text: Both methods converge on every dataset without divergent transitions. The conditional mean flow with the masked transformer has a lower NRMSE to the generating coefficients than the normalizing flow, its posterior draws reproduce the observed y t y_{t} more closely under the learned likelihood and the simulator ( Table 1 ), and its ESS per network evaluation is six times higher. However, each evaluation of the transformer is computationally more costly, such that the normalizing flow finishes sampling 22 × 22\times sooner, despite requiring more leapfrog steps inside NUTS.

sections.heading: Posterior predictive.
sections.text: Simulations from the learned likelihoods at posterior draws reveal the problem of sentinel values ( Figure 3 ). The predictive bands of the mean flow contract around the observed data at every observed time point. In contrast, the normalizing flow frequently generates the sentinel value − 1 -1 also at observed time points, which is reflected in a higher predictive RMSE ( Table 1 ). In summary, the flexible architecture of mean flows allows a masked transformer to marginalize missing observations. This yields a lower posterior error than a normalizing flow with sentinel values, but at a higher cost per density evaluation.

sections.heading: Setup and baseline.
sections.text: The g-and-k distribution is a standard benchmark with an intractable likelihood, defined through its quantile function ( Rayner and MacGillivray, 2002 ; Drovandi and Pettitt, 2011 ) . We use a bivariate version with a Gaussian copula and parameters ( g , k , ρ ) (g,k,\rho) , and datasets of N = 50 N{=}50 observations (Appendix E.2 ). The conditional mean flow learns the likelihood of a single observation, and we sample the posterior with NUTS. To assess whether a computational budget should be spent on more mean flow steps or on more posterior draws, we fix the product of requested draws per chain and network evaluations per density ( Appendix D ). Under this budget, we compare mean flow step counts S ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } S\in\{1,2,4,8\} with a normalizing flow. In addition, we evaluate delayed acceptance MCMC, which screens proposals with the mean flow at S c S_{c} steps and accepts them against a 100-step Tsit5 evaluation of the velocity head of the same network ( Section 3.2 and Appendix D ). A separately trained flow matching model integrated with 200 Euler steps serves as a baseline outside the budget, with 28 times more network evaluations.

sections.heading: Steps against draws.
sections.text: All mean flow settings converge on every dataset and reach a similar accuracy, with the lowest mean C2ST at S = 4 S{=}4 , although these differences are smaller than the spread across datasets ( Figure 4 A, Table S6 ). Fewer steps permit longer chains, and the minimum bulk ESS per network evaluation drops by an order of magnitude from S = 1 S{=}1 to S = 8 S{=}8 ( Figure 4 B–C). Hence, beyond S = 4 S{=}4 , a more accurate likelihood does not compensate for fewer posterior draws, and in practice, we recommend S = 2 S{=}2 for this benchmark. Under the same budget, the normalizing flow has a higher C2ST than every mean flow setting and requires more than four times the wall time of the mean flow ( S = 2 S{=}2 ; Figure S2 B). Regular flow matching also has a higher C2ST despite requiring more evaluations, and the same mean flow is about 50 × 50\times faster.

sections.heading: Delayed acceptance MCMC.
sections.text: Screening proposals with a coarse mean flow and accepting them against the fine evaluation of the same network gives an accuracy comparable to NUTS ( Table S6 ). With the coarse acceptance rate adapted to 0.3 0.3 , the fine level accepts 80 to 85% of the evaluated proposals, rising with S c S_{c} . Delayed acceptance MCMC is about 26–37 times faster than the flow matching baseline, but slower than NUTS with the mean flow likelihoods and yields a lower ESS. In summary, a few mean flow steps with more posterior draws give a lower posterior error than both the normalizing flow and the flow matching baseline, at lower wall time. Delayed acceptance MCMC with the same network gives comparable accuracy without gradients.

sections.heading: 5 DISCUSSION
sections.text: Neural density estimators for SBI have so far traded flexibility for fast density evaluation. Conditional mean flows relax this trade-off by allowing the step count to be chosen after training. In low-dimensional benchmarks, one or two steps matched the accuracy of flow matching while reducing MCMC time by up to two orders of magnitude. Few steps also yielded accurate posterior samples, and under a fixed MCMC budget, more draws were more valuable than more steps. Limitations. The main limitation is the cost of density evaluation in high dimensions. Each step requires its full Jacobian and a log-determinant, whose cost grows cubically with the dimension, and differentiating the log-determinant for NUTS involves second-order derivatives. Together with the higher cost of each transformer evaluation, this made MCMC in the renewal application slower than with the normalizing flow despite using fewer network evaluations. In addition, the cycle loss encourages but does not guarantee invertibility, so the learned densities may not exactly be normalized. Finally, the coverage of every method, including flow matching with 200 steps, decreased at large trial counts, consistent with error accumulation. Outlook. Beyond MCMC, fast mean flow densities can support self-consistency objectives ( Schmitt et al., 2024a ) and, together with prior and likelihood evaluations, evidence estimation ( Kucharský et al., 2026 ) . Since these methods also rely on repeated density evaluation, our work could make flexible flow-based estimators practical in any SBI setting that requires densities.

sections.heading: Appendix B Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: All experiments use 10 independent datasets, and we report the mean and standard deviation of the following metrics over datasets.

sections.heading: Classifier two-sample test (C2ST).
sections.text: The C2ST compares two distributions through a classification task ( Lopez-Paz and Oquab, 2017 ) . If the approximate and the reference posterior coincide, no classifier can tell their draws apart better than chance, whereas any difference between them can be exploited by a sufficiently flexible classifier. Hence, the held-out accuracy a ^ \hat{a} of a trained classifier measures how distinguishable the two distributions are: a ^ = 0.5 \hat{a}=0.5 indicates indistinguishable and a ^ = 1 \hat{a}=1 perfectly separable draws. We label approximate draws with 1 1 and reference draws with 0 0 , subsample both sets without replacement to the same size, which is fixed within each experiment across all methods and step counts, standardize the pooled draws, and train a classifier c ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) c(\bm{\theta})\in(0,1) with the binary cross-entropy. The classifier is an MLP with two residual hidden layers of width 2 ⌈ log 2 ⁡ ( 10 ​ D ) ⌉ 2^{\lceil\log_{2}(10D)\rceil} for D D -dimensional draws, Mish activations, dropout of 0.1 0.1 and a sigmoid output unit. We train it with AdamW (learning rate 5 × 10 − 4 5{\times}10^{-4} with linear warmup and cosine decay, weight decay 5 × 10 − 3 5{\times}10^{-3} , gradient clipping at norm 1.5 1.5 ) and batch size 128 for at most 100 epochs, with early stopping (patience 5) on 20% of the training data. The accuracy of the classifier c ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) c(\bm{\theta}) on held-out draws is averaged over 5-fold cross-validation.

sections.heading: Posterior predictive checks.
sections.text: For the DDM, we simulate a replicate dataset for each of 200 posterior draws and compare the observed choice proportion, the conditional response-time quantiles (10, 30, 50, 70 and 90%) and the timeout rate T T with their replicate distribution. For each summary, we compute the discrepancy z = ( T ⁡ ( 𝐲 obs ) − T ¯ rep ) / sd ⁡ ( T rep ) z=\big(T(\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{obs}})-\bar{T}_{\mathrm{rep}}\big)/\mathrm{sd}(T_{\mathrm{rep}}) and the predictive p p -value P ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 𝐲 rep ) ≥ T ⁡ ( 𝐲 obs ) ) P\big(T(\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{rep}})\geq T(\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{obs}})\big) , and report the largest | z | |z| across summaries.

sections.heading: Convergence diagnostics.
sections.text: We compute split- R ^ \hat{R} and bulk ESS following Vehtari et al. (2021) . A run passes our convergence criteria if max ⁡ R ^ ≤ 1.05 \max\hat{R}\leq 1.05 , the minimum bulk ESS is at least 100 and at least 500 draws are kept. Reported means and standard deviations include runs that fail these criteria.

sections.heading: Appendix C Architectures, Training and Hyperparameter Search
sections.text: All networks and diagnostics are implemented in BayesFlow 2.0.14 ( Radev et al., 2023 ; Kühmichel et al., 2026 ) , where we added the conditional mean flow as an additional inference network.

sections.heading: Architectures.
sections.text: • Mean flow: An MLP with 5 hidden layers of width 256. The condition 𝐱 \mathbf{x} is embedded by a linear layer and concatenated with the target 𝐳 \mathbf{z} at the input, and, together with a Fourier embedding with scale 0.3 0.3 of the time pair ( s , s − t ) (s,s-t) , it modulates every residual block ( Perez et al., 2018 ) . The auxiliary velocity head shares all but the last 2 layers. • Masked transformer: A transformer ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) with 5 blocks of width 128 and four attention heads. It tokenizes each observation and parameter and receives the time pair ( s , s − t ) (s,s-t) through adaptive layer normalization. During training, each observation of each simulation is dropped independently with probability 0.3, redrawn for every batch. Dropped tokens are excluded from attention and loss. A causal mask additionally restricts each observation token to parameter and observation tokens up to its own time step. The velocity head branches from the last 2 blocks and uses the same masks. Each observation and parameter token receives a learned embedding of its coordinate index, which for observations is the time step, and a Fourier embedding is used only for the time pair. • Consistency model: A continuous-time consistency model ( Lu and Song, 2025 ) with an MLP of 6 hidden layers of width 256. • Flow matching: An MLP with the same depth and width as the mean flow, without the velocity head. • Normalizing flow: A spline coupling flow ( Durkan et al., 2019 ) with 5 coupling layers, each with 2 hidden layers of width 256, and with 2 coupling layers, each with 2 hidden layers of width 128, for the renewal application.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: We trained all networks offline on standardized parameters and observations with a batch size of 256, using AdamW with weight decay 5 × 10 − 3 5{\times}10^{-3} , gradient clipping at norm 1.5 1.5 , and a learning rate warmed up linearly over the first 5% of steps from 5 × 10 − 5 5{\times}10^{-5} to 5 × 10 − 4 5{\times}10^{-4} and then decayed to zero with a cosine schedule. We used 50,176 simulations for two moons and the DDM, 100,000 for g-and-k, and 8,192 for the renewal model to compare architectures under limited data, with 1,024 further simulations for validation. The conditional mean flow, the consistency model, and the flow matching model were trained for 1,000 epochs, and the normalizing flow for 200 epochs with early stopping (patience 10).

sections.heading: Hyperparameter search.
sections.text: We selected the training hyperparameters of the conditional mean flow with a search in Optuna ( Akiba et al., 2019 ) on two benchmarks: two moons and a three-dimensional variant of the Gaussian linear task with uniform prior. Table S2 lists the search space and the selected values, which all experiments use. The training times are s = u s 1 + α s=u_{s}^{1+\alpha} and t = u t 1 + α t=u_{t}^{1+\alpha} with u s , u t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) u_{s},u_{t}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) , and for 0 0 unshared layers the velocity head reads the velocity from the boundary case 𝐮 𝝍 ​ ( 𝐳 , s , s , 𝐱 ) \mathbf{u}_{\bm{\psi}}(\mathbf{z},s,s,\mathbf{x}) . Each trial trained one network per benchmark for 250 epochs of 100 freshly simulated batches of size 256 and evaluated it with S = 4 S{=}4 steps on 256 held-out datasets with 500 posterior draws each. The score of a benchmark was the sum of an accuracy term, the calibration error, and the grid Hellinger distance to the exact posterior. The accuracy term is 2 ​ ( C2ST − 0.5 ) 2\,(\mathrm{C2ST}-0.5) on two moons and the NRMSE on the Gaussian task, and the calibration error is the median absolute difference between the nominal and empirical coverage of central credible intervals at 20 levels. The C2ST was averaged over 15 and the Hellinger distance over 3 of the held-out datasets. The search minimized the sum of both benchmark scores with the multivariate tree-structured Parzen estimator of Optuna ( Akiba et al., 2019 ) on 200 trials. sections.heading: Code.
sections.text: The code and the configurations of all experiments are available under the MIT license at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MeanFlow-AISTAST . The code is written in Python 3.14, and all networks are Keras 3.15.1 models ( Chollet and others, 2015 ) on the JAX 0.11.1 backend ( Bradbury et al., 2018 ) , both under the Apache 2.0 license. Besides BayesFlow (MIT), we build on PyMC 5.28.5 (Apache 2.0) ( Salvatier et al., 2016 ) and nutpie 0.16.11 (MIT) ( Seyboldt et al., 2026 ) for MCMC, ArviZ 0.23.4 (Apache 2.0) ( Martin et al., 2026 ) for the convergence diagnostics, and Optuna 4.9.0 (MIT) ( Akiba et al., 2019 ) for the hyperparameter searches.

sections.heading: Compute environment.
sections.text: We ran all analyses on a computing cluster using eight CPU cores and one NVIDIA A100 GPU with 40 GB of VRAM. The computing cluster uses an AMD EPYC 7F72 CPU with a core clock speed of up to 3.2 GHz and 50 GB of RAM.

sections.heading: NUTS.
sections.text: We sample with the NUTS implementation of nutpie ( Seyboldt et al., 2026 ) through PyMC ( Salvatier et al., 2016 ) on the JAX backend ( Bradbury et al., 2018 ) , with 4 chains, a diagonal mass matrix, a maximum tree depth of 10 and the default target acceptance rate of nutpie . We use the default of 400 warmup iterations, except for g-and-k, where the warmup is 25% of the requested draws of each method.

sections.heading: Budget on g-and-k.
sections.text: A method whose density costs K K network evaluations requests 8,000 / K 8{,}000/K draws per chain, so that the product of requested draws and network evaluations per density is constant across methods. The normalizing flow counts as K = 1 K{=}1 . For delayed acceptance MCMC, the requested iterations are 96,000 / ( J ​ S c + 100 ) 96{,}000/(JS_{c}+100) per chain, which accounts for the J = 5 J{=}5 coarse evaluations and one fine evaluation per iteration. The budget is set on the requested draws and ignores the number of leapfrog steps per draw, which differs between methods, so the realized number of network evaluations varies. We count one network evaluation per forward pass of the network for one pair ( 𝐳 , 𝐱 ) (\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x}) : a normalizing flow costs one evaluation per density, a mean flow with S S steps costs S S , a velocity field integrated with S S Euler steps costs S S , and a fixed-step Tsit5 integration costs 7 per step. Jacobians, divergences and gradients are obtained by automatic differentiation on top of these passes and are not counted; their cost is reflected in the wall times.

sections.heading: Delayed acceptance MCMC.
sections.text: We implement two-level delayed acceptance MCMC ( Christen and Fox, 2005 ) with the subchains of Lykkegaard et al. (2023) . For any coarse posterior π c \pi_{\mathrm{c}} , its invariant distribution is the fine posterior π f \pi_{\mathrm{f}} ( Section 3.2 ). Both levels use the same trained network: the coarse level evaluates the mean flow with S c ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } S_{c}\in\{1,2,4,8\} steps, and the fine level integrates its velocity head with 100 Tsit5 steps of fixed size and the exact divergence in ( 1 ). Each iteration runs a subchain of J = 5 J{=}5 random-walk Metropolis steps on π c \pi_{\mathrm{c}} , following Lykkegaard et al. (2023) , and proposes its end point to the fine level with the acceptance probability ( 11 ). The random walk draws Gaussian increments with a step size per parameter, initialized at 10% of the prior width, and a global scale. A proposal outside the prior’s support is rejected without evaluating the network. If the subchain does not move, the proposal equals the current state and is accepted without evaluating the fine likelihood. Adaptation takes 25% of the requested iterations and is discarded. During adaptation, a Robbins-Monro update steers the global scale towards a coarse acceptance rate of 0.3 0.3 , and in its second half, the step sizes are updated to the marginal standard deviations of the states visited in that half, after which the proposal is fixed. We run 4 chains started from prior draws.

sections.heading: E.1 Two Moons
sections.text: The prior is 𝜽 ∼ 𝒰 ​ ( − 1 , 1 ) 2 \bm{\theta}\sim\mathcal{U}(-1,1)^{2} , and the forward model is a \displaystyle a ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( − π / 2 , π / 2 ) , r ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0.1 , 0.01 2 ) , \displaystyle\sim\mathcal{U}(-\nicefrac{{\pi}}{{2}},\nicefrac{{\pi}}{{2}}),\qquad r\sim\mathcal{N}(0.1,0.01^{2}), 𝐲 \displaystyle\mathbf{y} = ( r cos a + 0.25 , r sin a ) + ( − | θ 1 + θ 2 | / 2 , ( − θ 1 + θ 2 ) / 2 ) , \displaystyle=\big(r\cos a+0.25,\;r\sin a\big)+\big({-}|\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}|/\sqrt{2},\;(-\theta_{1}+\theta_{2})/\sqrt{2}\big), whose fold makes the posterior invariant under ( θ 1 , θ 2 ) ↦ ( − θ 2 , − θ 1 ) (\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\mapsto(-\theta_{2},-\theta_{1}) , which gives two crescent-shaped modes ( Greenberg et al., 2019 ) . Since the density is available in closed form and the forward model can be inverted, we draw 32,000 exact i.i.d. reference samples per observation. The first dataset uses the canonical observation 𝐲 = ( 0 , 0 ) \mathbf{y}=(0,0) , and the other nine use prior predictive draws.

sections.heading: E.2 g-and-k
sections.text: The g-and-k distribution is defined by its quantile function in normal-score space ( Rayner and MacGillivray, 2002 ) , W ⁡ ( z , g , k ) = ( 1 + 0.8 ​ tanh ⁡ ( g ​ z / 2 ) ) ​ ( 1 + z 2 ) k ​ z , z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) , W(z;g,k)=\big(1+0.8\tanh(gz/2)\big)\,(1+z^{2})^{k}\,z,\qquad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), and has no closed-form density. Since W W is strictly increasing for k ≥ 0 k\geq 0 , we invert it by bisection, which gives the exact log-density by the change of variables. We couple two coordinates with a Gaussian copula of correlation ρ \rho in normal-score space, such that both marginals are g-and-k distributed. The priors are g ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( − 1 , 1 ) g\sim\mathcal{U}(-1,1) , k ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.5 ) k\sim\mathcal{U}(0,0.5) and ρ ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( − 0.9 , 0.9 ) \rho\sim\mathcal{U}(-0.9,0.9) , and each dataset consists of N = 50 N{=}50 observations simulated from a parameter drawn from the prior. We obtain 32,000 reference draws per dataset from an adaptive random-walk Metropolis ensemble on the exact log-posterior, started around the generating parameter with a jitter of 2% of the prior width (8 chains, 5,000 adaptation iterations, 40,000 draws thinned by 10, R ^ ≤ 1.05 \hat{R}\leq 1.05 and ESS ≥ 400 \geq 400 ).

sections.heading: E.3 Epidemic Renewal
sections.text: On a grid of T = 128 T=128 steps, of which the first n 0 = 5 n_{0}=5 are seeded at incidence I 1 = ⋯ = I n 0 = 10 I_{1}=\dots=I_{n_{0}}=10 and not observed, the renewal model is, for t > n 0 t>n_{0} , Λ t \displaystyle\Lambda_{t} = ∑ s = 1 15 w s ​ I t − s , I t = R t ​ Λ t ​ exp ⁡ ( σ p ​ ε t − 1 2 ​ σ p 2 ) , y t = log ⁡ I t + σ o ​ η t , \displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{s=1}^{15}w_{s}\,I_{t-s},\qquad I_{t}=R_{t}\,\Lambda_{t}\,\exp\!\big(\sigma_{p}\varepsilon_{t}-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_{p}^{2}\big),\qquad y_{t}=\log I_{t}+\sigma_{o}\eta_{t}, with ε t , η t ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \varepsilon_{t},\eta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) , σ p = σ o = 0.05 \sigma_{p}=\sigma_{o}=0.05 , and w w the Gamma density with mean 5.0 and standard deviation 2.5 ( Fraser, 2007 ; Cori et al., 2013 ) . This is the renewal equation of Cori et al. (2013) with a discretized generation interval truncated at 15 steps. The observation is ( y n 0 + 1 , … , y T ) (y_{n_{0}+1},\dots,y_{T}) , so d = 123 d=123 . The parameter is the whitened coefficient vector 𝐳 ∈ ℝ 128 \mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{128} with log ⁡ R = L ​ 𝐳 \log R=L\mathbf{z} , where L ​ L ⊤ LL^{\top} is a squared-exponential kernel with lengthscale 2.5, marginal standard deviation 0.4 and a 10 − 6 10^{-6} ridge ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2005 ) . Hence, the prior is exactly 𝐳 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\mathbf{I}) . Since L L is lower triangular, z s z_{s} enters log ⁡ R t \log R_{t} only for t ≥ s t\geq s , and since the recursion runs forward in time, y t y_{t} does not depend on z s z_{s} for s > t s>t . The causal attention mask of the masked transformer ( Appendix C ) encodes exactly this structure. Observations are standardized separately at each time step. We withhold each of the observed steps independently with probability 0.3 and draw a new pattern for every dataset. Since this mechanism is independent of the process and the parameters, the data are missing completely at random, and the posterior only requires the marginal likelihood p ⁡ ( 𝐲 𝒪 ∣ 𝐳 ) p(\mathbf{y}_{\mathcal{O}}\mid\mathbf{z}) of the observed entries 𝒪 \mathcal{O} ( Little and Rubin, 2019 ) . The masked transformer trains on complete simulations with masks drawn independently per simulation and observation at the same rate and thereby learns this marginal for every pattern. The normalizing flow instead models vectors with the sentinel − 1 -1 in the missing entries according to Wang et al. (2024) .

sections.heading: E.4 Cognitive Model
sections.text: A trial is a Wiener process with drift ν \nu that starts at β ​ a \beta a (with fixed relative starting point β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 ) and terminates at the first hit of 0 0 or a a . The response time adds a non-decision time t 0 t_{0} , and trials time out after 10 s 10\text{\,}\mathrm{s} . The priors are ν ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( − 3 , 3 ) \nu\sim\mathcal{U}(-3,3) , a ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0.8 , 2 ) a\sim\mathcal{U}(0.8,2) and t 0 ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0.1 , 0.4 ) t_{0}\sim\mathcal{U}(0.1,0.4) , and we simulate with Euler-Maruyama at d ​ t = 10 − 4 \mathrm{d}t=10^{-4} . The network observes the signed response time y = ( 2 ​ c − 1 ) ​ t y=(2c-1)\,t , with c = 1 c=1 for the upper boundary, which is bijective with the pair of response time and choice. Since the non-decision time cannot exceed the fastest observed response time, we sample it below this bound, which tightens as trials are added. Within each dataset, trial counts are nested, and every setting keeps 4 × 1,000 4\times 1{,}000 NUTS draws after the default warmup. For the first trial count N = 4 N{=}4 , the chains start at the center of the prior support with the default jitter of PyMC . The chains for the next trial count start at the posterior median of the preceding trial count, clipped to the current support of t 0 t_{0} , with independent jitter per chain.

Radev University of Bonn University of Bonn Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute Abstract Flow matching has emerged as a powerful generative family for simulation-based inference (SBI). However, sampling and density evaluation require numerical integration at inference time. This makes posterior sampling in neural posterior estimation costly. More importantly, it can make repeated likelihood evaluation prohibitively expensive and impractical for Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, which may require thousands of repeated density evaluations. Here, we develop conditional mean flows for posterior and likelihood approximation, combining few-step sampling with tractable density evaluation. We show that the mean flow objective identifies conditional flow maps and that independent masking enables direct estimation of marginal likelihoods. We evaluate both posterior and likelihood estimation across several tasks and show that conditional mean flows retain the flexibility of flow-based density estimators while significantly reducing inference time. In particular, single-step conditional mean flow density evaluation yields estimation error comparable to 200-step flow matching while enabling about 200-fold faster downstream MCMC sampling. 1 INTRODUCTION Mechanistic simulators are used to describe processes ranging from cognitive science ( Ratcliff et al., 2016 ) to disease modeling ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . Yet, while practically important, their likelihoods are often unavailable in closed form. Simulation-based inference ( Sisson et al., 2018 ; Cranmer et al., 2020 ; Deistler et al., 2025 ; Arruda et al., 2026 , SBI;) addresses this challenge by using simulated parameter-observation pairs ( 𝜽 , 𝐲 ) ( m{	heta},\mathbf{y}) to infer unknown parameters, and amortized methods reuse the trained network across datasets ( Bürkner et al., 2023 ) . Two popular forms of SBI are neural posterior estimation (NPE) and neural likelihood estimation (NLE). NPE learns a posterior model q 𝝍 ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 ) q_{ m{\psi}}( m{	heta}\mid\mathbf{y}) which can sample from the approximate posterior directly. NLE, instead, learns a likelihood model q 𝝍 ​ ( 𝐲 ∣ 𝜽 ) q_{ m{\psi}}(\mathbf{y}\mid m{	heta}) which requires Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample from the posterior. NPE amortizes over datasets but is usually tied to the prior and data format used in training, whereas NLE needs MCMC for every dataset, but allows the prior to be changed after training and composes exchangeable likelihoods across any number of i.i.d. observations ( Cranmer et al., 2020 ) . Many SBI methods demand neural estimators that are both flexible and inexpensive to evaluate. In NLE, MCMC requires thousands of likelihood evaluations per posterior, making each evaluation a practical bottleneck. Further, hierarchical approaches ( Arruda et al., 2024 ) or self-consistency objectives that improve NPE ( Schmitt et al., 2024a ; Mishra et al., 2026 ) and enable model comparison ( Kucharský and Bürkner, 2026 ) rely on density evaluation during training or inference. So far, normalizing flows have been a standard choice in these applications because they evaluate densities in a single pass ( Papamakarios et al., 2021 ; Dinh et al., 2017 ; Durkan et al., 2019 ) . However, their transformations must remain invertible with tractable Jacobians, which restricts how inductive biases can be built into the architecture ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Autoregressive flows based on causal transformers (e.g., TARFlow and STARFlow) relax this restriction ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) , but impose a fixed variable ordering and require sequential inversion for sampling. Moreover, tractable joint densities do not generally imply tractable marginals, which are required with missing observations ( Yalavarthi et al., 2024 ) . Flow matching and diffusion models instead learn a velocity or score field with an unconstrained neural network ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Wildberger et al., 2023 ; Sharrock et al., 2024 ; Arruda et al., 2026 ) , and diffusion transformers can flexibly represent arbitrary conditionals and marginals ( Gloeckler et al., 2024 ) . Yet, their densities require solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE), which can take hundreds of network evaluations and makes repeated likelihood calls during training or within MCMC costly. Few-step generative models reduce the sampling cost, but consistency models, for instance, provide no tractable density ( Song et al., 2023 ; Schmitt et al., 2024b ) . Thus, current SBI approaches either restrict the network architecture or make every density evaluation expensive . To overcome this limitation, we present conditional mean flows for SBI, which learn the average velocity between two times, so that one network evaluation defines a finite-time map based on mean flows ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ) . We first evaluate direct posterior sampling and density estimation, then focus on learned likelihoods for compositional inference, missing observations, and gradient-based and delayed acceptance MCMC. Concretely, we develop and showcase 1. a conditional mean flow formulation for posterior and likelihood approximation, with exact stepwise Jacobian determinants, and a proof that the mean flow objective suffices to identify conditional flow maps ( Section 3.1 , Proposition 1 ); 2. marginal density estimation for missing targets with a masked transformer backbone, and a proof that the masked objective targets the correct marginal likelihood ( Section 3.3 , Proposition 2 ); 3. and a benchmark against normalizing flows and regular flow matching on four tasks covering both NLE and NPE, including a single-trial likelihood comparison in which one mean flow step matches the error of 200-step flow matching with two orders of magnitude faster sampling ( Section 4 ); Figure 1: Learned two-moons posteriors as samplers and as densities. ( F ) The velocity head of the mean flow and ( G ) the flow matching model, both integrated with the adaptive Tsit5 ODE solver. 2 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK Simulation-based inference. For conditionally independent observations 𝐲 n \mathbf{y}_{n} , simulation-based inference targets p ⁡ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 obs ) ∝ p ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) ​ ∏ n = 1 N p ⁡ ( 𝐲 n ∣ 𝜽 ) p( m{	heta}\mid\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{obs}})\propto p( m{	heta})\,\prod_{n=1}^{N}p(\mathbf{y}_{n}\mid m{	heta}) when the likelihood is unavailable. Classical approximate Bayesian computation compares simulated and observed data directly, but becomes less effective as dimension increases ( Sisson et al., 2018 ) . Neural posterior estimation (NPE) fits q 𝝍 ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 ) q_{ m{\psi}}( m{	heta}\mid\mathbf{y}) to simulated pairs and draws approximate posterior samples without running MCMC for each dataset. Neural likelihood estimation (NLE), instead, fits a conditional density to prior-predictive pairs and uses it within MCMC ( Cranmer et al., 2020 , for an overview, see) . A per-observation estimator can be reused across dataset sizes, making single-trial likelihoods useful for models with exchangeable trials ( Boelts et al., 2022 ) , and spline coupling flows are the standard tractable-density baseline ( Durkan et al., 2019 ) . Flow matching and diffusion-based inference. Flow matching learns a velocity field 𝐯 ⁡ ( 𝐳 t , t ) \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) that transports a Gaussian distribution to the target along a prescribed interpolation ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) . It has been applied to both NPE and NLE, alongside score-based generative models ( Arruda et al., 2026 , for a review, see) . Sampling requires ODE integration, and density evaluation additionally integrates the velocity divergence through the continuous change-of-variables formula ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , so repeated integration can dominate the cost of NLE. Few-step generative models. Consistency models learn transitions from intermediate noisy states toward data, enabling generation in one or a few steps ( Song et al., 2023 ) . They also support fast posterior sampling in SBI ( Schmitt et al., 2024b ; Arruda et al., 2026 ) , although the standard formulation does not provide a tractable posterior density. Flow maps learn finite-time ODE transitions between arbitrary time pairs, and mean flows parameterize these maps through average velocities and can be trained without distillation ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ) . Rehman et al. (2026) combined mean flows with a cycle loss that encourages invertibility to obtain few-step densities for Boltzmann generators. MCMC with learned and multi-fidelity likelihoods. The no-U-turn sampler ( Hoffman and Gelman, 2014 ; Betancourt, 2017 , NUTS;) uses density and gradient evaluations to construct proposals, and probabilistic programming frameworks allow learned likelihoods to enter these calculations as model components ( Carpenter et al., 2017 ) . Delayed acceptance MCMC uses a cheap approximation to screen proposals while leaving the fine target invariant ( Christen and Fox, 2005 ) . Moreover, its multilevel variant organizes several approximations ( Lykkegaard et al., 2023 ) , and related approaches in SBI use simulators at different resolutions ( Prescott and Baker, 2021 ; Tatsuoka et al., 2026 ) . 3 METHOD A note on notation. The two moons task has a two-dimensional parameter and observation, a bimodal crescent posterior, and an exact likelihood and posterior sampler ( Greenberg et al., 2019 ; Lueckmann et al., 2021 ) . All methods learn the posterior direction and are sampled directly with 5,000 draws per dataset, which we score against 32,000 exact reference draws. We compare a conditional mean flow at step counts S ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } S\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} with three baselines: a conditional normalizing flow, a conditional consistency model as the established few-step method ( Song et al., 2023 ; Schmitt et al., 2024b ) , and a separately trained conditional flow matching model integrated with S S Euler steps or an adaptive Tsit5 solver ( Tsitouras, 2011 ) . We integrate the velocity head of the mean flow with the same Euler or adaptive scheme, which repurposes the mean flow as a flow matching model. For both the consistency model and the mean flow, we tuned the sampling schedule for each step count on held-out observations, which are disjoint from the evaluation datasets. Sample quality. The conditional mean flow reaches a similar C2ST at every step count ( Figure 1 and Figure S1 A), so a single step suffices for sampling and already outperforms the normalizing flow ( 0.523 0.523 against 0.543 0.543 ). In contrast, the consistency model needs at least 4 steps to approach this accuracy, and both flow matching variants need at least 32 Euler steps. The adaptive solver further improves the accuracy, but requires more than 300 solver steps. Hence, the mean flow with S = 1 S{=}1 draws 5,000 samples about 23 times faster than flow matching with 32 Euler steps and 140 times faster than with the adaptive solver ( Figure S2 ). It is also about 6 times faster than the normalizing flow and only reaches its sampling time at S = 8 S{=}8 . Since the velocity head of the mean flow and the separately trained model perform similarly under both solvers, mean flow training does not seem to degrade the learned velocity field. The consistency model is also sensitive to its discretization exponent, whose candidates span a C2ST from 0.54 0.54 to 0.98 0.98 at S = 4 S{=}4 , whereas the EDM schedule of the mean flow changes the C2ST by at most 0.015 0.015 ( Table S3 ). Density quality. In contrast to sampling, we find that additional mean flow steps improve the density, and the Hellinger distance to the exact posterior decreases with S S ( Figure S1 B and Table S4 ). With S = 1 S{=}1 , the mean flow places mass between the two modes ( Figure 1 C), but it still outperforms the normalizing flow. Euler integration of either velocity field remains less accurate than the mean flow with S ≥ 2 S{\geq}2 up to 32 steps. The adaptive solver is most accurate, with the velocity head of the mean flow ahead of the separately trained flow matching model. Moreover, the mean flow density is close to normalized, whereas the Euler densities overshoot unit mass by many orders of magnitude at S = 1 S{=}1 and remain far from normalized at S = 32 S{=}32 ( Table S4 ). We attribute this to the Euler scheme approximating both the trajectory and the divergence integral in ( 1 ), whereas the mean flow computes the exact Jacobian determinant of each step. The normalizing flow is exactly normalized, but its density shows fold artifacts and places mass outside the prior support ( Figure 1 A). Flow matching models with adaptive solvers provide the most accurate densities, but more than 300 steps per evaluation make them too expensive for repeated density evaluation. 4.2 Single-Step Likelihoods Yield Error Comparable to 200-Step Flow Matching Setup and baseline. The g-and-k distribution is a standard benchmark with an intractable likelihood, defined through its quantile function ( Rayner and MacGillivray, 2002 ; Drovandi and Pettitt, 2011 ) . The conditional mean flow learns the likelihood of a single observation, and we sample the posterior with NUTS. To assess whether a computational budget should be spent on more mean flow steps or on more posterior draws, we fix the product of requested draws per chain and network evaluations per density ( Appendix D ). Under this budget, we compare mean flow step counts S ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } S\in\{1,2,4,8\} with a normalizing flow. In addition, we evaluate delayed acceptance MCMC, which screens proposals with the mean flow at S c S_{c} steps and accepts them against a 100-step Tsit5 evaluation of the velocity head of the same network ( Section 3.2 and Appendix D ). A separately trained flow matching model integrated with 200 Euler steps serves as a baseline outside the budget, with 28 times more network evaluations. Steps against draws. All mean flow settings converge on every dataset and reach a similar accuracy, with the lowest mean C2ST at S = 4 S{=}4 , although these differences are smaller than the spread across datasets ( Figure 4 A, Table S6 ). Fewer steps permit longer chains, and the minimum bulk ESS per network evaluation drops by an order of magnitude from S = 1 S{=}1 to S = 8 S{=}8 ( Figure 4 B–C). Hence, beyond S = 4 S{=}4 , a more accurate likelihood does not compensate for fewer posterior draws, and in practice, we recommend S = 2 S{=}2 for this benchmark. Under the same budget, the normalizing flow has a higher C2ST than every mean flow setting and requires more than four times the wall time of the mean flow ( S = 2 S{=}2 ; Figure S2 B). Regular flow matching also has a higher C2ST despite requiring more evaluations, and the same mean flow is about 50 × 50	imes faster. Delayed acceptance MCMC. Screening proposals with a coarse mean flow and accepting them against the fine evaluation of the same network gives an accuracy comparable to NUTS ( Table S6 ). With the coarse acceptance rate adapted to 0.3 0.3 , the fine level accepts 80 to 85% of the evaluated proposals, rising with S c S_{c} . Delayed acceptance MCMC is about 26–37 times faster than the flow matching baseline, but slower than NUTS with the mean flow likelihoods and yields a lower ESS. In summary, a few mean flow steps with more posterior draws give a lower posterior error than both the normalizing flow and the flow matching baseline, at lower wall time.
